props.title: Accattone
props.initialSlug: A pimp's struggle for redemption in Rome's slums

sections.content: Accattone marks Pier Paolo Pasolini's explosive directorial debut, transforming Rome's impoverished streets into a neorealist canvas. Shot with documentary-like precision, it follows Vittorio "Accattone" Cataldi, a small-time pimp struggling in Rome's underworld. The film shares DNA with earlier neorealist masterpieces like Rome, Open City (1945) and La Strada (1954), but Pasolini's raw approach and use of non-professional actors pushes beyond their boundaries. His decision to score street scenes with Bach's sacred music creates a jarring, transcendent effect that influenced directors like Martin Scorsese, particularly in Mean Streets (1973).

sections.content: Pasolini's background as a poet and novelist shapes Accattone's unique visual language. Unlike the optimistic humanism of De Sica's Bicycle Thieves (1948), Pasolini presents an unflinching look at moral decay. The film's influence extends through Italian cinema, visible in the work of Bernardo Bertolucci's La Commare Secca (1962) and Marco Bellocchio's Fists in the Pocket (1965). The director's use of Roman dialect and street slang was revolutionary, breaking from the polished language of mainstream Italian cinema.

The film's religious imagery, particularly its Christ-like portrayal of its anti-hero, established themes Pasolini would explore throughout his career, reaching their apex in The Gospel According to St. Matthew (1964). This synthesis of sacred and profane elements influenced later directors like Abel Ferrara, especially in Bad Lieutenant (1992), and the Dardenne brothers' L'Enfant (2005). SUBHEAD: Impact on Social Realism

sections.content: Accattone's influence on social realist cinema cannot be overstated. Its DNA can be found in Ken Loach's Kes (1969), Alan Clarke's Made in Britain (1982), and more recently in the works of the Safdie brothers, particularly Heaven Knows What (2014). The film's unflinching portrayal of marginalized characters and its use of street casting created a template for authentic cinema that continues to resonate.
